title: Episode 66: The Scopes Monkey Trial: Darrow, Bryan, and the Battle of Dayton
description:
In July 1925, the sleepy mountain town of Dayton, Tennessee, became the arena for the most famous trial in American history. A young science teacher named John T. Scopes was tried for teaching Charles Darwin's theory of evolution under the Butler Act, bringing legendary defense attorney Clarence Darrow face-to-face with three-time presidential candidate William Jennings Bryan.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In the blistering summer of 1925, an extraordinary legal and philosophical battle erupted in the small Appalachian town of Dayton, Tennessee. At issue was a freshly passed state law prohibiting the teaching of human evolution in public schools. But what began as a staged publicity stunt to put a struggling coal town on the map quickly exploded into a titanic cultural war that transfixed the globe. The trial pitted two of the greatest oratorical titans of the twentieth century against one another: Clarence Darrow, the brilliant agnostic defense champion, and William Jennings Bryan, the beloved Christian fundamentalist crusader. George brings us the circus, the courtroom, and the ideas of the Scopes Monkey Trial.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE BUTLER ACT AND ROBINSON'S DRUGSTORE
In March nineteen twenty-five, Tennessee Governor Austin Peay signed into law the Butler Act, a statute that made it unlawful for any teacher in a state-funded school or university 'to teach any theory that denies the Story of the Divine Creation of man as taught in the Bible, and to teach instead that man has descended from a lower order of animals.' The American Civil Liberties Union in New York immediately placed advertisements in Tennessee newspapers, offering to finance the legal defense of any teacher willing to test the law's constitutionality. In early May, a group of prominent civic leaders in Dayton, Tennessee, gathered over lemonade at Robinson's Drugstore. The town's blast furnace had closed, and the local economy was languishing. Local manager George Rappleyea proposed an audacious scheme: if they could stage a high-profile test trial in Dayton, the publicity would bring thousands of visitors, journalists, and investment capital to their sleepy mountain community. They summoned twenty-four-year-old John Thomas Scopes, a popular, unassuming general science teacher and football coach at Rhea County High School. Scopes agreed to help, admitting that he had assigned chapters on Darwinian evolution from George William Hunter's textbook, Civic Biology. Scopes was promptly arrested, and the stage was set. Business owners in Dayton hoped that a high-profile legal showdown would revive the town economy, never anticipating that their modest community would become the ideological battlefield of the century. The dramatic events unfolded against a backdrop of deep cultural transformation, as rural communities confronted the rapid onset of modern industrial technology and national media attention. Dayton was a struggling former mining and agricultural town of eighteen hundred people, whose business leaders were desperate for any publicity that might attract outside industrial capital and tourists to Rhea County.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE GATHERING OF THE TITANS
What began as a localized promotional stunt instantly escalated into an international ideological arena. William Jennings Bryan, the three-time Democratic nominee for President of the United States, former Secretary of State, and America's most revered fundamentalist Christian orator, volunteered to lead the prosecution team. Bryan viewed Darwinian evolution as a dangerous, soulless philosophy of social Darwinism that undermined Christian morality, justified imperialist warfare, and eroded the democratic spirit of the common people. In response, Clarence Darrow, the nation's premier criminal defense lawyer and an outspoken agnostic who had famously defended labor leaders and Leopold and Loeb, volunteered his services for the defense free of charge. Darrow saw the trial as a crucial defense of intellectual freedom, academic liberty, and the separation of church and state against what he considered religious bigotry. The battle lines were drawn between two diametrically opposed visions of American civilization. Bryan arrived in Dayton wearing a white pith helmet and palm leaf fan, greeted at the train station by thousands of cheering Christian fundamentalists who viewed him as the defender of traditional American faith. Eyewitness accounts recorded in local diaries and regional newspapers captured the tension and uncertainty of the moment, preserving vivid details for future generations of historians. Clarence Darrow was the most renowned defense attorney in America, a towering agnostic champion of the labor movement and civil liberties who volunteered his services without fee to defend the freedom of academic inquiry.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE CARNIVAL IN RHEA COUNTY
In July nineteen twenty-five, Dayton was transformed into a sweltering, colorful carnival. Over two hundred journalists from across America and Europe packed the town's boarding houses, led by the acerbic, cynical social critic H.L. Mencken of the Baltimore Sun, who christened the proceedings the 'Monkey Trial.' Banners reading 'Read Your Bible Daily' hung between brick storefronts; street evangelists shouted from wooden crates on the courthouse lawn; patent medicine pitchmen sold miracle elixirs; and hot-dog vendors peddled concessions alongside performing chimpanzees in suits. The trial was the first in American history to be broadcast live over nationwide radio: microphones from Chicago station WGN sat on the judge's bench, transmitting the courtroom arguments to millions of listeners from coast to coast. Telegraph operators sent over two million words of dispatches over transatlantic cables, making Dayton the most talked-about town on Earth. Banners bearing biblical verses fluttered from telegraph poles along Market Street, while hot dog vendors and sidewalk performers sold miniature toy monkeys wearing spectacles to curious tourists. The stifling July humidity inside the crowded courtroom caused tempers to flare as defense attorneys argued that the Butler Act established a state-mandated religious orthodoxy that violated the First Amendment.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE COURTROOM CRUCIBLE
On Friday, July tenth, nineteen twenty-five, Judge John T. Raulston pounded his gavel in the second-floor courtroom of the Rhea County Courthouse. The courtroom was jammed with nearly a thousand spectators, sweltering in ninety-degree heat with ceiling fans whirring lazily above. Judge Raulston, a devout Christian who routinely opened court sessions with prayer, ruled against Darrow at nearly every turn. Crucially, Raulston excluded all expert scientific testimony, declaring that the opinions of evolutionary biologists, geologists, and theologians were irrelevant to the narrow legal question: did John Scopes teach that man descended from lower animals? Darrow was furious, his defense strategy seemingly eviscerated. Darrow delivered scathing, eloquent speeches defending intellectual inquiry, while Bryan thundered from the counsel table, declaring that the Christian parents of Tennessee had a sovereign democratic right to determine what was taught to their children with tax dollars. The courtroom was so packed with spectators that the floorboards groaned beneath the weight, forcing bailiffs to open tall windows to catch any faint breeze off the surrounding Cumberland hills. Darrow's methodical, surgical cross-examination held the packed crowd spellbound, exposing the intellectual contradictions in Bryan's literalist interpretations of biblical texts before an international press corps.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: BRYAN ON THE WITNESS STAND
On the seventh day of the trial, facing complete judicial defeat, Clarence Darrow executed the most audacious, unprecedented tactical maneuver in Anglo-American legal history: he called the prosecuting attorney, William Jennings Bryan, to the witness stand as an expert on the Bible. Fearing that the weight of the massive crowd would collapse the second-floor courtroom floorboards, Judge Raulston moved the proceedings outdoors to a wooden platform beneath the leafy oak trees on the courthouse lawn. Surrounded by two thousand spectators in the sweltering afternoon heat, Darrow questioned Bryan for two relentless hours. With surgical precision, Darrow interrogated Bryan on the literal interpretation of scripture: Did Jonah truly survive inside a big fish? Was Eve created from a literal human rib? Where did Cain get his wife? How did Joshua stop the sun if the Earth rotated on its axis? Bryan defended biblical literalism with passionate conviction, but under Darrow's relentless philosophical probing, Bryan conceded that the six days of creation in Genesis might have been vast geological epochs rather than twenty-four-hour periods. Fundamentalist spectators gasped; Bryan grew agitated, shouting that Darrow's sole purpose was to slur the Bible, while Darrow shouted back that he was defending human intelligence against ignorance. Under the shade of the grand oak trees on the courthouse lawn, Darrow cross-examination of Bryan became a legendary clash of legal philosophies that transfixed listeners gathered around living room radios nationwide. Bryan delivered a final address that received polite applause, but his exhausted physical appearance alarmed supporters, who watched the Great Commoner leave the courthouse looking pale and visibly aged.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE VERDICT AND THE DEATH OF THE GREAT COMMONER
The following morning, Judge Raulston abruptly halted the examination, ruling Bryan's testimony irrelevant and striking it from the official court record. Realizing that the trial had achieved its intellectual purpose, Darrow asked the jury to return a verdict of guilty so that the constitutional issues could be appealed to higher courts. On July twenty-first, after deliberating for barely nine minutes, the jury found John Scopes guilty of violating the Butler Act. Judge Raulston imposed a standard fine of one hundred dollars. Bryan, denied the opportunity to deliver his grand, five-day concluding oration that he intended as his life's masterwork, spent the next few days touring Tennessee, giving fiery speeches under the summer sun. Five days after the trial concluded, exhausted and suffering from undiagnosed diabetes, William Jennings Bryan lay down for an afternoon nap in Dayton and never woke up. The 'Great Commoner' had died in the town where he fought his final crusade. Bryan death just days after the trial conclusion cast a somber shadow over the nation, as millions mourned the passing of the Great Commoner who had championed the common people for four decades. The courage and resilience demonstrated by everyday citizens during this critical trial inspired observers across the country, showing that ordinary people can rise to meet extraordinary challenges. The legal technicality spared Scopes from serving jail time and prevented the Supreme Court from ruling on the constitutional validity of anti-evolution statutes for another four decades.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE IMMORTAL LEGACY OF DAYTON
In nineteen twenty-seven, the Tennessee Supreme Court overturned Scopes's conviction on a technicality—Judge Raulston had set the hundred-dollar fine rather than the jury—preventing the case from reaching the United States Supreme Court. The Butler Act remained on Tennessee's law books until it was quietly repealed by the legislature in nineteen sixty-seven, one year before the Supreme Court struck down all similar bans nationwide in Epperson v. Arkansas. John Scopes left teaching, earned a graduate degree in geology from the University of Chicago, and spent a successful career as an oil and gas geologist in Texas and Louisiana, living a quiet life of personal integrity. Today, the Rhea County Courthouse in Dayton is a National Historic Landmark, where the original courtroom is restored to its 1925 appearance, flanked by statues of both Clarence Darrow and William Jennings Bryan on the lawn. The trial remains an immortal milestone in American cultural history: a poignant, colorful testament to the perennial struggle between faith and science, tradition and progress, and the enduring quest for intellectual freedom. The Rhea County Courthouse stands today as a monument to intellectual inquiry, where the delicate balance between religious faith and scientific discovery was debated with unforgettable passion and eloquence. Today, historic markers and museum collections honor these legendary figures, reminding us that the spirit of American adventure and perseverance continues to guide our shared journey forward. The Scopes trial became an immortal cultural touchstone in American legal and social history, immortalized in the play Inherit the Wind and symbolizing the enduring dialogue between scientific reason and religious tradition.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Scopes Monkey Trial proved that ideas have consequences that echo far beyond the courthouse walls. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we journey back to the eighteenth century for the forgotten fourteenth American state: the Lost State of Franklin.
